items_missed: No agenda statement at all — opened with 'Einstein moving Zachary speaking. How can I help you?' and then let the customer drive the entire call structure. No roadmap, no 10-15 minute timeframe, no 'sound good?'

Never asked for or used the customer's name. Vance gave it in his first sentence and Zachary used it zero times in 8.9 minutes. The customer had to ask 'And who am I speaking with again?' near the end, which is the tell that the open and the rapport were both thin.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up question.
No stairs or floors question at either address — on a 2400 sqft house and an unseen Arlington destination.
No question about garage, attic, storage closets, patio or balcony contents — only the rented storage unit came up, and only because the customer raised it.
No special-considerations probe — long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns, driveway access for a 26-foot truck at a new-construction ranch.
Never asked about packing services or quoted them, even after Vance said 'I'll need help getting the TVs off the walls and getting them prepared properly.'
Never asked how many boxes they have or will have.
No access probe — parking, gate codes, HOA restrictions at either end.
No moving-stressor question. Vance signaled his stressor twice ('how much it costs is what it comes down to for me', 'trying to keep the cost down') and it was never named or acknowledged.

Vance asked for a retired-military discount twice — 'I'm retired military so I'll take any discount I can get' and 'I'm obviously an old guy, I'll take any discounts' — and Zachary answered neither time. He went straight into the hourly rate.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener.
Never said what's included — gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools. Quoted a bare hourly number.
Never said disassembly and reassembly are included, despite Vance raising TVs coming off walls, couch backs coming apart, and 'a big, big freaking table that's heavy.'
No No Worries Damage Coverage mention — no $2,000, no 60c/lb baseline — on a call where the customer was openly worried about a tightly packed truck and things shifting.
No Meet Your Mover.
No On-Time Guarantee.
No 'no hidden fees' pitch — no credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no transportation or assembly fees.
Clock section almost entirely absent: never said the clock starts on site when the contract opens, never stated the 2.5-hour minimum, never explained 15-minute prorated increments.
Gave a point estimate ('around eight and a half hours') instead of a typical time range for a 2400 sqft home.
No specialty-item handling discussion for the king bed, two large reclining couches, or the heavy table.
No walk-distance, traffic, or equivalents (school bus reference) framing to make the estimate concrete.

Entire Save Your Ass speech missing. Vance handed him the setup — he is self-packing, his wife is working the bedroom, he has a pickup truck making trips, and he plans to take the wardrobes himself — and Zachary responded with 'Okay' and 'Right.' No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill', no consolidation examples, no take-a-carload tip, no sense-check.

No attempt to book. Both the load date and both delivery dates were confirmed available, the customer was flexible and warm, and Zachary still closed with 'when you're ready to pull the trigger' and let Vance say 'I'll give you a call back.' Never asked to lock it in.
No confirmation-email handoff, no bolded-details list, no 'reply with any corrections.' The only thing sent was the walkthrough link, and he said it goes to the cellphone.
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' and never gave hours or how to reach the branch.

No Sparefoot or Ecobox referral, even though the call opened with the customer needing third-party storage — Zachary said 'you would rent on your own' and left it there. He got lucky Vance already had a unit.
Significant cross-talk — at least four interruptions and two abandoned sentences ('And then to answer.', 'Now that dead.').
top_strength: Zachary is genuinely strong on logistics and pricing mechanics. He explained truck capacity in a way the customer could act on — one size truck, 26-foot box, roughly 1700 sqft each, so a 2400 sqft fully furnished home typically needs two — and then used that to offer the virtual walkthrough as the way to find out if it can be scaled to one. He handled the trip fee cleanly ($110 per truck, framed as a one-time fee to bring the empty trucks back to Frisco), and he was responsive on budget without being asked twice: when Vance pushed on cost, Zachary volunteered the smaller-crew comparison ($306/hr for three, $204/hr for two) so the customer could see the lever. He also proactively de-risked the estimate with 'should they beat the estimate or your move simply not take that long, that is all you'll pay for just the time actually worked.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix is the Save Your Ass speech, and this call is the cleanest example of why. Vance told you he is packing himself, his wife is on the bedroom, he has a pickup truck making trips, and he plans to carry his own wardrobes — then told you twice that cost is the deciding factor. That is a customer begging to be coached. The line was: 'Vance, since you're already packing, let me tell you how to save real money here — every box you consolidate and every carload you take yourself comes straight off the clock, so get the kids' stuff and the loose drawer items boxed, take the small breakables and the wardrobes in your truck, and pull the photos off the walls. On a move this size that can knock an hour or more off the bill. Does that make sense?' Second priority: use his name and open with an agenda. You never said 'Vance' once, and he had to ask your name at the end of the call — that costs you the relationship you need to close. Open with 'I'll grab some details about your move, then walk you through pricing, takes about ten to fifteen minutes, sound good?' Third: you left every differentiator on the table — no No Worries coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, no what's-included, no no-hidden-fees — so this quote is competing on price alone against a customer who is shopping on price. THREE LIVE BUSINESS RISKS. (1) This is really two moves — load-to-storage on the 8th and storage-to-Arlington on the 17th or 18th — and the '$3,600' was never scoped to one leg or both. Vance repeated it back as his number ('Okay, alright, oh, that's 3600'). If he shows up on the 17th expecting that to be covered, that is a billing dispute. Confirm in writing which leg the estimate covers and quote the second leg separately. (2) When Vance asked 'the travel time doesn't count against me, you said, right?' you answered 'Right, no, it's just a one time fee.' He is 47 miles from the destination — that loaded drive is on the clock inside the 8.5 hours. As answered, he believes he is not billed for driving. Correct that with him before he books. (3) You quoted the 2.5-hour-minimum-based hourly structure without ever stating the 2.5-hour minimum or the 15-minute prorated increments, and you anchored a dollar figure on a 2400 sqft home before the walkthrough came back. Because this was a walkthrough-scheduler call, sections 3 through 6 would normally be lighter — but you chose to quote pricing and a full dollar estimate on this call, so those sections were graded as they applied, and the retired-military discount question needs an actual answer either way.
phone_presence_notes: Friendly, patient and responsive on the substance, and the customer stayed upbeat throughout, but it was transactional — zero name use, repeated cross-talk, and two clear rapport openings (the retired-military ask and 'I'm obviously an old guy') went completely unacknowledged.
